latin: Carolus Magnus<sup>1</sup> corpore fuit amplō atque rōbustō, statūrā ēminentī<sup>2</sup> quae tamen jūstam nōn excēderet<sup>3</sup>...
apice<sup>4</sup> capitis rotundō, oculīs praegrandibus<sup>5</sup> ac vegetīs, nāsō paululum mediocritātem excēdentī, cānitiē<sup>6</sup> pulchrā, faciē laetā et hilarī<sup>7</sup>.
Exercēbātur adsiduē equitandō et vēnandō<sup>8</sup>... dēlectābātur frequentī natātū<sup>9</sup>.
Nec patriō tantum<sup>10</sup> sermōne<sup>11</sup> contentus, etiam peregrīnīs linguīs ēdiscendīs operam impendit<sup>12</sup>...
in quibus Latīnam ita didicit ut aequē<sup>13</sup> illa ac patriā linguā ōrāre<sup>14</sup> sit solitus<sup>15</sup>.
Graecam vērō melius intellegere quam prōnūntiāre poterat.
Dēlectābātur librīs Sānctī Augustīnī praecipuēque hīs quī Dē Cīvitāte Deī praetitulātī sunt.
Artēs līberālēs studiōsissimē coluit eārumque doctōrēs plūrimum venerātus magnīs adficiēbat honōribus...
Temptābat et scrībere<sup>16</sup>, sed parum successit labor praeposterus<sup>17</sup> et sērō<sup>18</sup> inchoātus<sup>19</sup>...

in quibus Latī́nam ita dídicit ut aequē<sup>13</sup> illa ac pátriā linguā ōrā́re<sup>14</sup> sit sólitus<sup>15</sup>.
Graecam vērō mélius intellégere quam prōnūntiā́re póterat.

Artēs līberā́lēs studiōsíssimē cóluit eārúmque doctṓrēs plū́rimum venerā́tus magnīs adficiḗbat honṓribus...
Temptā́bat et scrī́bere<sup>16</sup>, sed parum succéssit labor praepósterus<sup>17</sup> et sērō<sup>18</sup> inchoā́tus<sup>19</sup>...
english: Charlemagne [had a large and robust frame] (by body was large and robust), of a tall stature which nevertheless did not exceed the right [measure]...
the crown of the head rounded, the eyes very large and lively, the nose slightly exceeding the average, beautiful white hair, a joyful and smiling face.
He trained assiduously [in] riding and hunting (by riding and by hunting)... [he often gave himself up to the pleasure of swimming] (he was delighted by frequent swimming).
Not content [only] (so much) [to speak his] native language, he [also applied himself] (gave labour) to studying foreign languages...
[among] which he learnt [Latin] so well that he was in the habit of speaking it [as well as] his native language.
But he [understood] Greek better than he could speak it.
He [loved] (was delighted by) the books of Saint Augustine, in particular [the one] which [is] entitled The City of God.
He cultivated the liberal arts passionately, and, respecting greatly [those who taught them] (their teachers), he granted them great honours...
He also tried to write, but this work, which came at the wrong time and was begun late, had little success...

footnotes: Magnus, -a, -um, great, glorious; great in size is said procerus.

Corpore amplo, statura eminenti, etc.: here we have a whole series of adverbial complements of quality in the ABLATIVE. Do you remember canis brevibus cruribus from lesson 25? Emineo, -es, -ere, eminui, v. i., to project, to stand above.
Excederet: imperfect subjunctive of excedo, -is, -ere, cessi, cessum, to exceed.
Apex, apicis, m., summit: a term used in the same sense in mathematics and cosmography.
Prae + abl., preposition, in front, in preference to..., also serves to form a kind of superlative: praegrandis, -e = grandissimus, -a, -um.
Canus, -a, -um, white; is only said of the hair and the beard. Whence canities, -ei, f., which is a less annoying consequence of age than calvities (cf. L. 39, N. 5).
Facies, -ei, f., face, figure. Hilaris, -e, smiling.
Equitare, to ride on horseback; venari, to hunt; equitando, venando, ablative of the gerund, by riding, by hunting.
Natatus, -us, swimming; from natare, a verb also found in a shorter form: no, nas, nare, navi, v. i.
Tantum, adv., so much, so; non (nec) tantum sed etiam, is a frequent phrase (vid. sup. L. 53, N. 2).
Sermo, -onis, m., language; in the same sense one will find below: patria lingua.
Impendo, -is, -ere, pendi, pensum, to devote to, to spend on something.
Aequus, -a, -um, equal (in all senses of this word); aeque, equally. We have already seen aequalis, -e, equal (in size, in age); aeque... ac, in the same way as; simul... ac, at the same time as.
Oro, -as, -are, to speak; whence orator, orator.

Sit solitus = solitus sit, perfect of the semi-deponent verb: soleo, -es, -ere, solitus sum, to be in the habit of... The passive form above therefore has an active (intransitive) sense. Cf. Old French SOULOIR: «Deux parts en fit dont il soulait passer / L'une à dormir et l'autre à ne rien faire» (La Fontaine).
Et scribere: when et does not link two words to one another, it means also; but the second et in sentence 9 links two adjectives: it therefore has its normal sense.

Posterus, which comes after (post + acc., after); postero die, the next day; posteritas, the future, descendants. For the use of prae, vid. sup. N. 5. In praeposterus, which comes at the wrong time, lit. that which should have come behind, prae nevertheless does not have the same value as in praegrandis: it is the opposition between prae and post that suggests the idea of bad timing.
Inchoare, to begin, to sketch out. We will speak to you before long about «inchoative verbs».
comments: Do grammatical notes bore you? Although grammar can, we think, be a very interesting thing, we understand perfectly that you may not yet be convinced of it.

If that is the case, take them only in small doses, but fairly often. Little by little you will understand their interest and usefulness. You can, of course, learn Latin as many radio enthusiasts have learnt radio: by practice alone. By soldering away and modifying their circuits until they seemed to work more or less correctly, they have sometimes obtained astonishing results. But in radio-electricity as in Latin, a little theoretical knowledge makes it possible to save considerable time, while broadening one's culture. Now grammar is to the practice of languages what mathematics is to applied techniques: one must not abuse it, but a minimum is necessary to get out of the rut of routine.
Today the lesson is easy. If you have a moment of leisure left, do not forget to repeat the Latin text of the previous lesson, trying not to look at the translation.
And do not forget the 2nd wave: today you should revise the 4th lesson.

Accidit, impersonal verb, it happens or it has happened; the present and the past have the same form: you can deduce from this that this verb belongs to the 3rd conjugation. — Gypsum, -i, n., plaster. — Natalicius, -a, -um, relating to birth (here, understood: of Christ); natalicia, -orum, pl. n., birthday. — Frango, -is, -ere, fregi, fractum, to break, to fracture.

CURIOSITY (thing to be noted). — Extract from the dictionary of Du Cange, Paris, 1733: «E glossario Du Cange, Lutetiae Parisiorum anno 1733° edito, excerptum: Narta, species solearum lignearum quibus in transmittenda glacie altissimisque nivibus utuntur [...] Finni aliaeque gentes finitimae. Nihil aliud sunt [...] quam lignum tenue et longiusculum, anteriore sui parte incurvum, in cujus medietate ansa est ex corio, cui pes inseritur, subjecta ex contorto vimine alia, qua posteriora pedis firmantur.» — Narta, kind of wooden sandals which the Finns and other neighbouring peoples use to move over the ice and (very) deep snow. They are nothing other than a [piece of] narrow, fairly long wood, curved at its front part, in the middle of which there is a [strap] (handle) of leather into which the foot is slipped, [and another] of twisted [wicker] (vimen, -inis, n.), [on] which the heels are held.

Here you have the proof that our NARTA, which must have surprised you (E. 53, P. 9), was not chosen lightly: our earliest reference dates from 1733, and at that time this word had already proved itself long since.

latin: Quid tibi accidit? Cūr crūs gypsō alligātum est?
Hoc Fēriīs Nātālīcīs accidit. In Alpibus nartābam et pessimē cecidī.
Ita est. Duōs mēnsēs cum crūre gypsō vestītō agam oportet; priōrem mēnsem in lectō ēgī.
Nunc ambulāre possum sed magna cum cautiōne: semper mihi cavendum est nē cadam.
Quā rē natandō exercērī nōn potes.
Errās! Nōnnūllius est mōmentī. In urbe nostrā omnibus annī temporibus natāre possumus: piscīna mūnicipālis hieme calefit.
latinAccented: Quid tibi áccidit? Cūr crūs gypsō alligā́tum est?
Hoc Fḗriīs Nātālī́cīs áccidit. In Álpibus nartā́bam et péssimē cécidī.
Ita est. Duōs mēnsēs cum crūre gypsō vestī́tō agam opórtet; priṓrem mēnsem in lectō ēgī.
Nunc ambulā́re possum sed magna cum cautiṓne: semper mihi cavéndum est nē cadam.
Quā rē natándō exercḗrī nōn potes.
Errās! Nōnnū́llius est mōméntī. In urbe nostrā ómnibus annī tempóribus natā́re póssumus: piscī́na mūnicipā́lis híeme cálefit.
english: What happened to you? Why is [your] leg in plaster (with plaster bound)?
It happened at Christmas (at the Christmas holidays). I was skiing in the Alps and [had a very bad fall] (I fell very badly).
Yes. I have to spend two months with my leg in plaster (dressed in plaster); I have already spent the first month in bed.
Now I can walk, but with great caution: I must always [take care] not to fall.
[So] (by which thing) you won't be able to train at swimming.
That's of no importance: we are in winter!
You're wrong! It is of some importance. In our town, one can swim [all year round] (in all the seasons of the year): the municipal swimming pool is heated in winter.
